opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons, and they connect to each other.

The first is simply that the public, and policymakers in particular, need to make decisions about a technology whose risks are hard to perceive directly. Most people interact with AI through a chatbot that's helpful and polite, and it's very natural to conclude from that experience that there's nothing much to worry about. But the concerns many of us have, like systems developing goals we didn't intend, deceptive behavior, self-preservation tendencies, or misuse for things like cyberattacks or biological weapons, aren't visible in everyday use. They show up in carefully designed experiments, under specific conditions, and often only in the most capable systems. So if we want democratic societies to make informed choices, someone has to run those experiments and show the results in a way people can understand.

The second reason is that the companies are the ones who have the access. They have the frontier models, the compute, and the internal knowledge of how the systems were trained. Academic researchers and independent organizations can do some of this work, but they're often a step or two behind the frontier and have limited resources. So there's a kind of responsibility that comes with being at the frontier: if you're building something that you yourself say could carry serious risks, you should also invest in helping everyone else understand those risks, not just in mitigating them quietly behind closed doors.

Third, I think it's actually in the companies' long-term interest, even if it doesn't always feel that way in the short term. Trust is going to be essential. If the public later discovers that dangers were known internally and not communicated, the backlash could be severe and the regulation that follows could be much less thoughtful. Whereas if companies are seen as being transparent and contributing to a shared, evidence-based understanding, that builds the kind of legitimacy you need to operate a powerful technology in a society.

And finally, there's a scientific point. A lot of the debate about AI risk has been somewhat abstract: arguments, thought experiments, intuitions. That's important, but we also need empirical grounding. When you can demonstrate, concretely, that a model will, for example, try to avoid being shut down or will mislead its evaluators under certain pressures, it changes the conversation. It moves it from "this is speculative" to "this is a phenomenon we can study, measure, and hopefully fix." That's healthier for everyone, including people who are skeptical of the risks, because it gives them something real to engage with.

Of course, this has to be done responsibly. You don't want to publish a recipe for misuse in the name of public awareness. But I think the balance today is tilted far too much toward secrecy and toward the race for capabilities, and much too little toward helping society understand what's at stake.

r001.rationale: The response says public-facing experiments can build trust and improve informed decisions, and notes a race for capabilities. It does not say that improving public understanding would change the competitive dynamics companies face.

r002.rationale: The response mentions secrecy and competitive pressure, but does not state that these pressures can trap leading companies despite their good intentions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that these companies are in a very privileged position. They have the models, they have the compute, they have the people who understand the systems best. And right now a lot of the most important questions about risk — can a model deceive its evaluators, will it pursue goals we didn't give it, how fast are these dangerous capabilities emerging — those questions can only really be answered by running experiments on frontier systems. Academics like me can speculate, we can build theory, but we often can't test it at scale. So if the labs don't do these experiments, nobody does.

The second thing is that public understanding matters enormously for how this all goes. Governments are going to make decisions about regulation, about international agreements, and they will make those decisions based on what they believe the risks are. If the evidence is unclear, or if it's locked inside companies, then policy will be driven by intuition and by lobbying rather than by science. I think that's dangerous in both directions. We could over-react, or more likely in my view, we could under-react because the people with the clearest picture of the risks have commercial reasons to downplay them.

And honestly, there's a self-interest argument too. These companies say they want to be trusted. Trust comes from transparency. If you run an experiment that shows a model behaving deceptively in some setting, and you publish it, that's uncomfortable, but it builds credibility. It tells the public and regulators that you're taking this seriously, that you're not just saying "trust us." We've seen some of this already with the work on sleeper agents, on alignment faking, on evaluation awareness. Those papers changed the conversation. They made abstract worries concrete.

I'd add one more thing. I've changed my own mind over the last few years, partly because of evidence. I used to think the catastrophic scenarios were quite far off. What moved me was seeing the pace of progress and seeing early signs of exactly the kinds of behaviours we were worried about. If that kind of evidence can move a researcher who has spent his whole career in this field, imagine what it could do for policymakers who are still deciding whether this is science fiction. The experiments aren't just about satisfying curiosity. They're how a civilization figures out, collectively, what it's dealing with before it's too late to act.

r001.rationale: The response says public understanding can shape policy and build trust, but does not identify it as a way to change the companies’ competitive dynamics.

r002.rationale: It mentions commercial reasons to downplay risks, but does not say competitive pressures can trap companies despite good intentions.

astra-6.text:
I think the companies developing these systems have a responsibility to help society understand the risks. They have access to models and expertise that most researchers and members of the public don’t have. And there are important questions we can investigate experimentally, rather than simply arguing about whether we should be optimistic or pessimistic.

For example, under what conditions might a system deceive a human evaluator? How effective are the safeguards intended to prevent dangerous uses? We need evidence about these things, including evidence that our current concerns are mistaken or that particular protections actually work.

But the experiments have to be credible. If a company controls the research and only publishes reassuring results, we haven’t learned very much. Independent researchers need meaningful access, and findings need to be communicated honestly, with their uncertainties.

Ultimately, decisions about acceptable risk affect everyone. They shouldn’t be made only by the people building the technology. Better public understanding gives citizens and governments a stronger basis for making those decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says companies should help society understand AI risks, but does not connect this to changing the competitive dynamics they face.

r002.rationale: The response does not say competitive pressures can trap companies, even when they have good intentions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the companies building these systems have a responsibility to help society understand what the risks are. They have access to models and technical expertise that most people outside those companies don’t have. So they’re in a position to support experiments that make some of these questions more concrete: What can the systems actually do? Under what conditions do safeguards fail? And how much confidence should we have in the results?

But it’s important that this isn’t just a public relations exercise. Independent researchers need to be involved, and findings need to be shared even when they’re inconvenient for the company. The purpose should be to improve our understanding, including understanding where our concerns might be mistaken.

Ultimately, decisions about acceptable risk affect everybody. They shouldn’t be made only by the people developing the technology. Giving the public better evidence is part of making meaningful democratic oversight possible.

r001.rationale: The response argues that companies should help the public understand AI risks, but does not connect that effort to changing the competitive dynamics companies face.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that competitive pressures can trap companies despite their good intentions.
